items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: Weekly downloads 11,161, up 7% today and up 147% since the 4,518 recorded nine days ago. Stars moved 0% and forks 1.1% in the same window. Six appearances and the gap has widened on every one of them — attention flat, installation compounding. Ordinarily downloads follow stars; here they have decoupled entirely, and that decoupling is the single most useful pattern this list has produced so far.
items.description: A Python charting library, from the team behind the Reflex web framework.

items.name: AntigmaLabs/ante
items.brief: Stars up 14.1% and forks up 10.2% while HackerNews went the other way — front page presence gone entirely, posts down 33%, comments up 1.1%. The thread ended and the growth did not, which is the transition worth watching for and the second repo this month to show it. 34 forks on 1,443 stars is a modest 2.4% ratio, so the people arriving are mostly still evaluating rather than building on it.
items.description: A self-contained harness for running AI coding agents in a terminal.

items.name: antirez/h3.c
items.brief: Stars up 117% and forks up 96% in a single day, with open issues up 183% and HackerNews comments up 453% — every number roughly doubling or better at once. That is what a well-known author shipping something looks like on day one, and the honest caveat is that reputation drives the first day. What makes it worth watching rather than merely noting: 71 forks on 1,432 stars is already a 5% ratio, and 13 open issues means people are running it on their own machines within hours, not reading the README. The test is whether that holds when the name stops carrying it.
items.description: An inference engine written in C that runs the MiniMax H3 language model on Mac hardware, from the author of Redis.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: Weekly downloads 9,386, up 11.2% today and more than doubled since the 4,518 recorded four days ago. Stars moved 1.6% in the same window — downloads are now growing seven times faster than attention, which is the inversion this list exists to catch. Fifth appearance and the gap has widened each time. Whatever is happening here is happening in package managers, not on forums.
items.description: A Python charting library, from the team behind the Reflex web framework.

items.name: anthropic.com
items.brief: On HackerNews and Lobsters simultaneously, with Lobsters comments up 75% and points up 47.4%, HackerNews comments up 45%. Anthropic is not rising in any meaningful sense, so read this as a single announcement landing across two developer communities on the same day — a genuine launch wave, which the bucket rules correctly count as one kind of evidence rather than two.
items.description: Anthropic, the AI research company behind the Claude models.

items.name: antonz.org
items.brief: Lobsters comments up 112.5% and points up 22% — comments rising five times faster than points, which is the ratio that separates a post people argue with from one they simply approve of. A blog about Go and SQL internals landing that way usually means it made a claim about how a database actually behaves. Its traffic rank moved 0.7%, which is nothing; the discussion is the entire signal here.
items.description: The blog of Anton Zhiyanov, writing about Go, SQL and database internals.

items.name: palamim/starboard
items.brief: Second appearance and every number moved the same direction again — stars 3.1%, forks 3.6%, open issues 20%. Modest, consistent, and pushed today rather than abandoned after the thread. On a 156-star repo these are a handful of people, but they are the same handful coming back, which at this size is all the evidence available.
items.description: A Mac terminal that lives permanently beside the Dock rather than appearing on a hotkey.

items.name: CopilotKit/channels-sdk
items.brief: 824 stars with 54 forks and only 4 open issues — a fork ratio of 6.5% against almost no reported problems, which is unusual and reads two ways: either it works cleanly or nobody is pushing it hard enough to break it. Four days since the last push and growth has flattened to 1% on both stars and forks. Here because GitHub and HackerNews agree, not because anything is accelerating.
items.description: A toolkit for adding AI assistants into applications across chat, voice and other channels.

items.name: bbc.com
items.brief: HackerNews comments up 286.9% to 471 on a single story. The BBC is obviously not rising, and this entry exists to show what the corroboration rule does with a big established site: three collectors saw movement, the rule fired honestly, and the reading is simply that one story landed hard. Worth including because a list that silently drops its own false positives is harder to trust than one that explains them.
items.description: The British Broadcasting Corporation's news site.

items.name: MakazhanAlpamys/Soup
items.brief: 68 open issues against 430 stars — a 16% ratio, roughly five times what a healthy young repo shows, and forks up 5.5% against 3% star growth. Both point the same way: the people arriving are running it and hitting walls, not bookmarking it. For a tool claiming to fine-tune an 8-billion-parameter model on ordinary hardware, hitting walls is exactly what you would expect and exactly what makes the claim testable. HackerNews has gone quiet at 0.7%, so this is now growing without a thread pushing it.
items.description: Fine-tunes large language models from a single configuration file, streaming layers so an 8-billion-parameter model fits on ordinary hardware.

items.name: palamim/starboard
items.brief: Stars up 4.9%, forks up 6.7%, open issues up 20% — modest across the board and consistent in direction, which on a 144-star repo means a handful of real users rather than a crowd. A terminal pinned beside the Dock is a narrow idea with an obvious audience, and the fork-to-star ratio suggests some of them are already changing it. Two days since the last push.
items.description: A Mac terminal that lives permanently beside the Dock rather than appearing on a hotkey.

items.name: t8y2/dbx
items.brief: Third appearance. 13,242 stars with 1,344 forks and 1,117 open issues is an unusual shape — one fork per ten stars where most repos manage one in fifty — and that ratio has held steady across a week rather than spiking and fading. The Homebrew route remains the thing to watch: a package-manager install is somebody putting it on their machine, which is the only adoption a desktop database client can honestly claim.
items.description: A 20 MB cross-platform desktop client for querying more than 70 kinds of database from one window.

items.name: arcprize.org
items.brief: 470 HackerNews comments, the second-largest thread this week, on a benchmark designed to measure reasoning rather than memorisation. Comments up only 2.2% and best rank down 38.8%, so the thread has peaked — what puts this here is the size of the discussion, not its growth. A benchmark that provokes 470 comments is usually being argued about rather than adopted, and the useful question is whether anyone builds against it.
items.description: The ARC Prize, a competition and benchmark for measuring genuine reasoning in AI systems rather than memorisation.

items.name: leonickson1/Swiftlet
items.brief: Third day, and the story is that it has stopped being a story. Stars up 2.1% and forks 2.4% — matched, modest, and a long way from the 13.2% fork surge two days ago. Open issues actually fell 25%, meaning the maintainer is clearing them faster than new ones arrive. That is a healthy repo and no longer a rising one, which is worth saying plainly rather than dressing up.
items.description: A lightweight Swift web framework for building server-side applications.

items.name: bobdahacker.com
items.brief: A security researcher's site, on Lobsters with comments up 3.8% and points up 2.5%, alongside a 1.3% move in its traffic rank. Small numbers in every direction. It is here because three independent collectors saw it on the same day, which is the bar this list sets — but nothing about the magnitude says anything is happening yet.
items.description: The site of a security researcher who publishes findings from breaking into consumer products and services.

items.name: runtimewire.com
items.brief: Worth a line for what it is rather than how it moved: a startup-intelligence service tracking AI funding rounds, which is a direct competitor to what this project is building. Pricing tiers up 33.3% means it added a plan — the monetisation signal the guide calls a binary riser trigger. On the HackerNews front page with 22 comments.
items.description: A startup-intelligence service tracking funding rounds and company activity in AI.

items.name: xoreaxeaxeax/asm-hall-of-shame
items.brief: Stars up 38.4% in a day, forks up 12% and open issues up 20%, with GitHub, HackerNews and Lobsters all seeing it at once — three independent collectors and the widest star jump on today's list. Lobsters points more than doubled, up 108.8%, which for that community's size means it landed with almost everyone who saw it. A catalogue of the worst instructions in CPU history is the kind of thing that either gets ignored or gets contributed to, and 5 forks on 567 stars this early leans towards the second.
items.description: A catalogue of the worst-performing machine instructions across CPU designs, collected by a well-known reverse engineer.

items.name: jj-vcs/jj
items.brief: Second appearance. Jujutsu at 30,887 stars is long past discovery, so what is being tracked is not whether it grows but whether Git users actually switch — and Homebrew installs are the only honest measure of that. Forks and issues barely moved today; the entry earns its place through three unrelated collectors agreeing, not through any single number.
items.description: Jujutsu, a version-control system that works with existing Git repositories but replaces Git's commands with a simpler model.

items.name: V4bel/Zapscape
items.brief: Three independent collectors on day one — GitHub, HackerNews and Lobsters — which is rare enough to be the story on its own. Stars and forks both up 12.9%, moving in exact lockstep, and Lobsters comments up 25%. Appearing on both developer communities simultaneously usually means a security tool that does something people immediately recognise as either useful or alarming; 10 forks on 110 stars suggests they are running it to find out.
items.description: A security research tool for finding and mapping vulnerabilities in networked systems.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: Weekly downloads up 9.7% while the week-over-week growth figure itself jumped 342% — the acceleration is accelerating, which is the rarer of the two readings. 4,518 downloads a week now against 1,621 stars means more people are installing it than have bothered to bookmark it, and that ratio almost never runs this way round. 82 open issues on a library this young is the healthy kind of noise. Fourth appearance and the first where downloads, not attention, are doing the work.
items.description: A Python charting library, from the team behind the Reflex web framework.

items.name: FedericoTs/quantprobe
items.brief: Downloads at 1,555 a week but week-over-week growth is NEGATIVE 55%, which is the honest reading: the launch spike is over. Stars still up 4.5%, so attention has not caught up with the decline yet. Worth a line because the idea is good — telling you whether a 110-billion-parameter model will run on your laptop before you download 60 GB — and worth watching to see whether it finds a floor or keeps sliding.
items.description: Works out whether a large language model will actually run on your machine, and how fast, before you download it.

items.name: jj-vcs/jj
items.brief: 30,874 stars and 1,167 forks, so this is not new — Jujutsu has been the most credible attempt at replacing Git's interface for two years. What moved today is Homebrew installs, up 4.7%, alongside Lobsters points up 18.9%. The Homebrew number is the one that matters: a package-manager install is somebody putting it on their machine, not starring it in a browser tab, and for a version-control system that is the only adoption that counts.
items.description: Jujutsu, a version-control system that works with existing Git repositories but replaces Git's commands with a simpler model.

items.name: pg83/shitty
items.brief: Fourth day, and the shape has not broken. Open issues up 42.9% against 2% star growth — a ratio that says the people who arrived are using it hard enough to file bugs, long after HackerNews stopped talking (comments moved 1.2%). Most launch-driven repos flatten within seventy-two hours. This one has kept the adoption after losing the audience, which is the transition worth watching for.
items.description: A terminal emulator written from scratch, aiming for speed and a small codebase.

items.name: hisham.hm
items.brief: On Lobsters rather than HackerNews, with comments up 9.1% and points up 2.6% — small numbers from the invite-only community, which is the point of watching it. Hisham Muhammad wrote htop, so attention here is a known-quantity author being read rather than a discovery. On the list because two independent collectors saw it, which is the honest reason.
items.description: The personal site of Hisham Muhammad, who wrote htop, the process viewer most Linux users reach for first.

items.name: pg83/shitty
items.brief: Third appearance, and this is where a thread and a trend separate. Stars up 6.7% and open issues up 16.7%, while HackerNews comments moved 0.6% — the discussion has stopped and the adoption has not. That is the transition most launches never make, and for a terminal emulator with a deliberately absurd name it is more than it had any right to expect.
items.description: A terminal emulator written from scratch, aiming for speed and a small codebase.

items.name: leonickson1/Swiftlet
items.brief: Forks up 13.2% against 3.6% star growth — nearly four to one, and the widest gap on today's list. That ratio is the one worth trusting: a star is a bookmark, a fork is somebody starting work. 310 HackerNews points against 140 comments is a low argument ratio for a web framework, which usually means people found it plausible rather than provocative. Open issues up 16.7% on 434 stars says the forks are being run, not admired.
items.description: A lightweight Swift web framework for building server-side applications.

items.name: veedstudio/open-edit
items.brief: Second day on the list and the ratios held: stars up 8.2%, forks up 12.1%, with forks again outpacing stars. Yesterday the base was 141 stars and 8 forks, today 172 and 12 — small enough that a dozen people move it, so read the direction and not the magnitude. HackerNews comments up 60% on seven comments is noise; the fork growth is not.
items.description: An open-source video editor you install rather than subscribe to, designed to be driven by a coding agent.

items.name: googleworkspace/cli
items.brief: GitHub, Homebrew and npm all seeing it at once — three independent collectors, and Homebrew is the one that matters. A package manager entry means somebody installed it on purpose rather than starring it in a browser tab. Google shipping an official CLI for Drive, Gmail and Calendar replaces a decade of community scripts, so the interesting question is not whether it grows but what it kills.
items.description: Google's own command-line tool for Drive, Gmail and Calendar, replacing a dozen separate scripts.

items.name: fogus.me
items.brief: 487 HackerNews comments, the largest thread on today's list, from the blog of a programming-language designer who worked on Clojure. Comments up 145% but best rank down 85.7% — the post is being argued about long after it left the front page, which is a different shape from a post that is merely popular. Worth reading; not yet evidence about the site.
items.description: The blog of Michael Fogus, a programming-language designer who worked on Clojure.

items.name: veedstudio/open-edit
items.brief: Stars up 14.7% and forks up 17.9% on the same day, from a base of 141 and 8 — small enough that a handful of people move the percentages, so read the direction rather than the size. What makes it worth a line is the pitch: a video editor you own instead of rent, driven by a coding agent. That is two trends arriving at once, and it is day one on this list.
items.description: An open-source video editor you install rather than subscribe to, designed to be driven by a coding agent.

items.name: garagehq/nightcrawler
items.brief: Forks jumped 32.7% against 23.3% star growth in a day, and watchers rose 25% — three ratios moving together, which is rarer and harder to fake than any one of them spiking. 44 forks on 593 stars is a 7% ratio on a repo this small, meaning the people finding it are running it rather than filing it. A local AI red-teamer that works on a phone is a specific enough claim to attract either real users or real scepticism, and the 34 comments against 118 HackerNews points suggest more of the first.
items.description: A security testing tool that runs an AI red-teamer locally on a phone rather than in the cloud.

items.name: brian-armstrong/fec
items.brief: A Rust library for forward error correction, on the list with GitHub and HackerNews agreeing. Error-correction code is infrastructure nobody adopts casually — it either solves a problem someone has or it sits unused — so the thing to watch is not stars but whether anyone depends on it. No package downloads yet, which is the number that would turn this from interesting to real.
items.description: A Rust library for forward error correction — recovering data damaged in transmission without asking for it again.

items.name: rust-lang.org
items.brief: On the front page of HackerNews and Lobsters at the same time, with Lobsters comments up 1100% and points up 300%. Two independent developer communities is the corroboration this list exists to find — but Rust is not rising, it arrived years ago. What moved is one announcement, and the honest reading is that something specific happened today rather than that the language is growing.
items.description: The official site of Rust, a systems programming language designed for memory safety without a garbage collector.

items.name: chipsandcheese.com
items.brief: HackerNews comments up 1700% and best rank up 48.5%, on a publication doing deep processor analysis. The percentage is enormous because the base was one comment, so this is a single post landing rather than a trend — the useful question is whether the rank holds next week once the thread is gone, which is exactly what a daily time-series is for.
items.description: A publication doing deep technical analysis of computer processors and hardware architecture.

items.name: 0xchasercat/draco
items.brief: A drop-in replacement for Firecrawl, which is a paid crawling service — so this is the open-source-undercuts-incumbent shape, and those either die quietly or move fast. At 67 stars it is far too early to call, but open issues jumped 50% today against 2.8% star growth, meaning the few people who found it are using it hard enough to break it. Two days since the last push.
items.description: An open-source web crawler for AI applications, built as a drop-in replacement for the paid Firecrawl service.

items.name: pg83/shitty
items.brief: A terminal emulator whose HackerNews thread drew 160 comments against 172 points — a 93% comment-to-point ratio, roughly triple what a well-received post produces. That shape means argument, not applause, and for a terminal emulator the argument is always the same one: whether the world needs another. Stars up 5.7% and forks up 5.4% on the same day says some readers stopped arguing and cloned it.
items.description: A terminal emulator written from scratch, aiming for speed and a small codebase.

items.name: drumih/turbo-fieldfare
items.brief: Stars have more than doubled in five days, 2,196 to 4,945, and forks are still outpacing them — 7.8% against 5.6% in the last day alone. Open issues rose 11.6% in the same window, which on a young repo means people hitting real edges rather than admiring the README. Five days on this list and the ratios have not softened, which is the part that separates a thread from a trend.
items.description: Runs Google's Gemma 4 language model on a MacBook in about 2 GB of memory, rather than requiring a server.

items.name: t8y2/dbx
items.brief: 1,344 forks and 1,117 open issues against 13,242 stars, which is an extraordinarily engaged ratio — one fork for every ten stars, where most repos manage one in fifty. The signal today is not the star count but Homebrew: it is installable through a package manager, which is the point a tool stops being a repo people star and becomes one they run. Downloads up 2% week over week is modest, and the install path is the thing to watch.
items.description: A 20 MB cross-platform desktop client for querying more than 70 kinds of database from one window.

items.name: wie-project/kakehashi
items.brief: A userspace translation layer letting macOS binaries run on Linux ARM64 — technically the hardest kind of project on this list and the kind that usually stalls. 252 HackerNews points against 64 comments is an unusually low argument ratio, which for infrastructure means people are impressed rather than sceptical. 341 stars is small; the engineering claim is what makes it worth watching.
items.description: A translation layer that lets software built for macOS run on Linux machines with ARM processors.

items.name: simonwillison.net
items.brief: HackerNews comments up 600% and best rank improved 55.8%, on a personal blog that posts about AI tooling almost daily. This is a well-known writer, so the reading is not "an unknown is rising" — it is that a specific post landed hard enough to move the numbers of a site that is usually steady. Worth reading the post, not tracking the domain.
items.description: The weblog of Simon Willison, co-creator of the Django web framework, covering AI tooling and software engineering almost daily.

items.name: pudding.cool
items.brief: The Pudding, a visual-essay publication, with 157 HackerNews comments and its best rank up 23.3%. Comments are actually down 16% from the previous window, so the thread is past its peak; what put this here is the rank move, which follows front-page placement rather than leading it. Attention, not adoption.
items.description: The Pudding, a publication that explains cultural and social questions through interactive visual essays.

items.name: drumih/turbo-fieldfare
items.brief: Forks are growing faster than stars — 10.1% against 8.3% — which is the ratio that separates a tool people run from one they bookmark, and 231 forks on 4,671 stars is high for a repo this young. The HackerNews thread drew 343 comments against 913 points, a 38% ratio meaning argument rather than applause; for a claim about fitting Gemma 4 into 2 GB, the argument is the story. Pushed today, so the maintainer is still in it.
items.description: Runs Google's Gemma 4 language model on a MacBook in about 2 GB of memory, rather than requiring a server.

items.name: ssp.sh
items.brief: A data-engineering blog whose HackerNews numbers moved 20% on a base of four points. The percentage is real and the base is far too small to carry it — this is here because two unrelated collectors happened to see it, not because anything large happened. Worth a second look only if it returns later in the week.
items.description: A blog on data engineering — pipelines, warehouses and the tooling around them — written by one practitioner.

items.name: Claude Opus 5
items.brief: Third on ProductHunt with 450 votes, and the only launch today carrying independent search demand alongside it. That distinction matters more than the rank: a launch is something that happens to a product, while search interest is people going looking of their own accord, and it is the harder of the two to manufacture. Read the search signal, treat the vote count as the noise around it.
items.description: Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 language model, launched on ProductHunt.

items.name: type.today
items.brief: A foundry cataloguing fonts built for contemporary typesetting, on the HackerNews front page today with 31 comments. Its traffic rank moved 1.2% in the same window, and that is almost certainly the front page rather than anything independent — front-page placement sends a spike that a popularity ranking then registers. One event seen twice, not two events.
items.description: A type foundry and catalogue of fonts chosen for contemporary typesetting, with writing on typography.

items.name: diataxis.fr
items.brief: Diátaxis is a framework for structuring technical documentation into four modes, and it drew 59 HackerNews comments today. The 0.9% move in its traffic rank arrived alongside that thread rather than before it, so this is attention rather than adoption — the useful question is whether the rank holds next week once the thread is gone. That test is exactly what a daily time-series is for.
items.description: A framework for organising technical documentation into four distinct modes: tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation.

items.name: worksinprogress.news
items.brief: A magazine covering underrated ideas in science and policy, with 59 HackerNews comments today. Same shape as the other front-page domains on this list: real discussion, a half-percent nudge to its traffic rank, and no evidence yet that separates a good post from a growing publication.
items.description: An online magazine covering underrated ideas in science, technology and public policy.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: Fourth day on the list and the only entry today confirmed by three unrelated collectors — npm downloads, GitHub stars and HackerNews. Downloads are up 41% week over week against 4.4% star growth, and 65 open issues on 1,296 stars is a high ratio: people are running it in anger rather than admiring it. The watcher count sits at 3, which is the one discordant note — almost nobody has committed to following the project despite using it.
items.description: A Python charting library, from the team behind the Reflex web framework.

items.name: mokshablr/gander
items.brief: 207 HackerNews points and 75 comments against 287 stars and 4 forks. Attention running well ahead of adoption: a lot of people read about it, very few took it home. Stars grew 7.4% and forks 9.1% overnight, so the gap is closing slowly rather than not at all. It has already left the front page, which makes the next two days the test.
items.description: An Android file viewer for PDF, Word, Excel and PowerPoint that works offline and asks for no permissions.

items.name: createcentercv.org
items.brief: Movement across three independent readings — Majestic, OpenPageRank and Tranco — but all of it small: rank up 5%, subnets up 1.4%. The value here is the agreement rather than the size. Three unrelated crawls noticing the same modest climb is a different claim from one crawl noticing a big one.
items.description: A youth-safeguarding charity in Cape Verde working on child protection and community programmes.

items.name: wikif1.org
items.brief: An F1 wiki with 1.5% rank movement and 1% subnet growth. Genuinely marginal — it clears the corroboration bar because two independent sources both registered the same small climb. Listed for honesty about what today's threshold admits.
items.description: An independent Formula 1 reference site — standings, schedules and race results, not affiliated with F1.

items.name: playscrabble.com
items.brief: Same shape as createcentercv: three sources, all agreeing, none dramatic. Rank up 5.4% with subnets up 2%. A long-established word-game site — this is what steady looks like, and it is here to show that the corroboration rule fires on ordinary movement too, not only on spikes.
items.description: A long-running free Scrabble site where people play each other online.

items.name: mondomedia.com
items.brief: Referring IPs up 29% and subnets up 28% — one new link per network, which is the healthy shape. Rank change of 35% on an established media domain. The near-identical IP and subnet growth is what genuine link acquisition looks like and is the clearest contrast on this page with the Omsk entry.
items.description: The publisher behind Happy Tree Friends and Dick Figures — adult animated shorts, online since the 1990s.

items.name: drumih/turbo-fieldfare
items.brief: Third day climbing and the shape got better, not worse: stars up 25% to 3,848 while forks rose 33% and open issues 58%. Forks and issues both outpacing stars means people are running the code and hitting real edges, not bookmarking it. HackerNews has gone quiet — comments up only 1.5%, off the front page — so this is now growing on its own without a thread pushing it, which is the transition most launches never make.
items.description: Runs Google's Gemma 4 language model on a MacBook in about 2 GB of memory, rather than requiring a server.

items.name: DramaWave - Dramas & Reels
items.brief: DramaWave improved its best rank 20% to position 12 while falling 34% in the US, 32% in the UK and 22% in Germany. Charting far better overall while losing every tracked Western market means the gain came from somewhere we do not watch. With 100 million Android installs already, this is a mature short-drama app moving on ad spend, not a discovery.
items.description: A short-form vertical drama streaming app — soap-opera episodes shot for phones, in the same category as ReelShort.

items.name: FORScan Lite - for Ford, Mazda
items.brief: FORScan Lite's Android installs jumped to 10 million and reviews rose 57% in a day — an enormous move for a paid car-diagnostics tool with only 192 iOS ratings. The install figure is bucketed by Google, so a jump like that is a threshold being crossed rather than a real overnight surge. Worth watching the review count instead: 57% growth there is a genuine number.
items.description: Car diagnostics for Ford, Mazda and Lincoln vehicles, reading fault codes an ordinary OBD2 scanner cannot.

items.name: yc-software/qm
items.brief: Stars up 121% and forks up 150% in a day, with open issues up 124% and its HackerNews rank improving sharply. Forks growing faster than stars on a repo this young means people are cloning to modify rather than to watch. Everything about it is early enough that a single day could reverse it, but the fork-to-star ratio is the healthiest in today's set.
items.description: A tool for running several AI coding agents on the same task at once.

items.name: Freecash - Get Paid Real Money
items.brief: Freecash improved its best rank 7% while slipping in the UK and US. Paid-reward apps move on marketing budget rather than product quality, so read this as an advertising signal. It has appeared in this set three days running with the same pattern, which makes it a good control: if the system flags it every day, its threshold for apps is probably still a touch loose.
items.description: Pays people small amounts to complete offers, surveys and game milestones. Reward-app category, ad-funded.

items.name: sqliteai/waste
items.brief: Stars up 74% and forks up 69% while comments more than doubled to 161 against just 9 points. That comment-to-point ratio is still inverted — roughly eighteen comments per point — which means the discussion is an argument, not applause. Yesterday's question was whether the stars were the idea or the fight; two days of doubling suggests the idea is surviving the fight.
items.description: Runs a 2.78-trillion-parameter model on hardware that cannot hold it, by streaming weights off an SSD as they are needed. A small C engine with no dependencies.

items.name: hillelwayne.com
items.brief: 106 HackerNews comments and a small Tranco improvement. Same shape as maurycyz.com: an individual writer having a good day. The value here is the reverse of a riser — it tells you what developers are arguing about today, which is a content signal rather than a company signal.

items.name: projectpluto.com
items.brief: 79 comments on the front page with a 0.6% Tranco move. Astronomy software with a long history. The pattern across today's domain set is clear and worth naming: HackerNews plus a tiny traffic bump almost always means one popular post, not a rising business.

items.name: seriot.ch
items.brief: HackerNews points up 20% from a base of 4, with one comment. This is noise that cleared the bar because the domain population was quiet. Listed so the set stays honest about what qualified rather than quietly dropping it.

items.name: chriscoyier.net
items.brief: 52 comments, front page, 0.6% traffic gain. Chris Coyier is a well-known web developer; this is his personal site. Fourth example of the same shape today, which is a stronger argument for a gate rule about personal blogs than it is about any of these four domains.

items.name: maurycyz.com
items.brief: HackerNews comments up 156% to 180 with its front-page rank improving 12%. A personal site pulling that much discussion is usually one essay landing rather than a site becoming popular. Worth reading what it published today; not worth tracking the domain.

items.name: drumih/turbo-fieldfare
items.brief: Grew from 2,196 to 3,038 stars overnight — 36% — with forks up 42%, and it did that after leaving the HackerNews front page. Attention there has flattened to 1% growth while the repo itself keeps climbing, which is the split that matters: the launch is over and the growth did not stop with it. Open issues up 22% says people are running it and hitting real edges, not just bookmarking.
items.description: Runs Google's Gemma 4 language model on a MacBook in about 2 GB of memory, rather than requiring a server.

items.name: marbleos.com
items.brief: HackerNews points up 2,100% to 108 with 65 comments, front page, and nothing else in the system has seen it. This is the earliest shape RiseFinder can detect and also the least proven — one well-received post produces exactly this. Worth a look precisely because it is undecided.

items.name: reclip.io
items.brief: Four points, no comments. It clears the bar only because the domain population barely moved today. Nothing to act on.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: The first thing this system has confirmed from three unrelated places at once — npm downloads, GitHub stars, HackerNews. Downloads are up 139% week over week against 9.9% star growth, so it is being installed far faster than it is being admired, and 64 open issues on 1,119 stars means those installs are hitting production. Watch the issue count: at this ratio the maintainer's response time decides whether it keeps the users it is winning.
items.description: A Python charting library, from the team behind the Reflex web framework.

items.name: orangecrumbs.com
items.brief: Three points, no comments, same story as reclip.io. Listed for completeness; a quiet day makes small numbers rank well.

items.name: sqliteai/waste
items.brief: 75 comments against 9 points is an eight-to-one ratio, and that only happens when people are arguing. Stars still more than doubled and forks rose 86%, so the argument is drawing builders rather than repelling them. It is on the front page now, which means tomorrow tells you whether the stars were the idea or the fight.
items.description: Runs a 2.78-trillion-parameter model on hardware that cannot hold it, by streaming weights off an SSD as they are needed. A small C engine with no dependencies.

items.name: sawfwair/mere-run
items.brief: 41 stars, 14 points, 7 comments, and it has already fallen off the front page. It ranks here only because percentile scoring is relative and the population was quiet — a handful of people account for every number on this line. No conviction; listed so the set is honest about what cleared the bar.

items.name: SerhiiKorniienko/bullshit-detector
items.brief: Yesterday this was up 141% on stars and 3,200% on comments; today it is up 5%. The spike is over and it converted very little — 90 stars and 4 forks from 68 comments of discussion. Comments still run level with points, so it remained an argument to the end rather than a tool anyone adopted.

items.name: gavamedia/deltafin
items.brief: Forks up 20% and open issues up 40% against 11.9% star growth — the third day running that usage has outpaced attention on this one. Six open issues on 567 stars is still a clean tracker, so the friction is early rather than accumulating. The HackerNews points reading dropped to zero while 87 comments remain, which is more likely a flagged post than a collapse in interest.

items.name: DramaWave - Dramas & Reels
items.brief: DramaWave improved its best rank 5% while losing ground in Germany, the UK and the US at once — 16% in the US alone. That combination only works if it is charting hard in a market outside the four tracked here. Same short-drama category as DramaBox and the same read: watch the category, not the app.
items.description: A short-form vertical drama streaming app — soap-opera episodes shot for phones, in the same category as ReelShort.

items.name: Reelo - Media Hub
items.brief: Reelo holds rank 7 on a paid chart with 10 ratings and 5,000 Android installs. Those numbers do not belong together: a paid chart position that high on that little evidence usually means a thin category rather than a real hit. It slipped in both the UK and US today. Treat as a category artefact until a second source says otherwise.

items.name: Claude by Anthropic
items.brief: Claude reversed yesterday's slide, gaining 7.6% in Japan and about 1.5% in both the UK and US while holding second place overall. Yesterday it was losing ground in exactly the markets it gained in today, which usually means a short campaign or a news cycle rather than anything structural. Two days does not make a trend, but the direction flipped cleanly.

items.name: LukeTandjung/base-gpui
items.brief: Comments up 66.7% against 4.7% star growth, on a 45-star repo. Everything about this is small enough that a handful of people account for all of it. It scores highly only because percentile ranking is relative — in a quiet population, modest movement ranks well. Worth one more day before treating it as anything.

items.name: drumih/turbo-fieldfare
items.brief: Forks grew 41.5% in a day against 18.6% star growth — people are copying it to build on roughly twice as fast as they are bookmarking it, which is the healthier of the two ratios. At 2,196 stars with 326 HackerNews comments it is past the point where a single post explains the numbers. It has already left the front page, so the next two days separate a launch spike from a tool that stuck.
items.description: Runs Google's Gemma 4 language model on a MacBook in about 2 GB of memory, rather than requiring a server.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: Forks up 17.9% and open issues up 25.5% against only 8.5% star growth. The same shape as deltafin: usage outpacing attention. At 1,007 stars with 59 open issues this is a project being deployed rather than starred, and the 46 HackerNews comments suggest the discussion is technical rather than promotional.
items.description: A Python charting library, from the team behind the Reflex web framework.

items.name: openai/codex-security
items.brief: Still climbing three days after first appearing: stars up 18.8% and forks up 18.3% in the last twenty-four hours, now at 7,237 and 472. It remains on the HackerNews front page with 197 comments. Sustained growth at this size is the strongest pattern in today's set — most launches decay by day three, and this one has not.

items.name: alibaba/skill-up
items.brief: Modest movement — 5% star growth on a 296-star repo, with HackerNews points up 66.7% from a base of three. Included because it is corporate-backed rather than independent, which changes what the growth means: an Alibaba repo does not need HackerNews to find users, so early external interest here is a weaker signal than the same numbers on an unknown project.

items.name: gavamedia/deltafin
items.brief: Open issues jumped 300% while forks rose 26.8% and stars 15.2%. Issue counts growing faster than stars means people are running it and hitting problems, not admiring the README. That friction is a better adoption signal than a clean tracker, though it also means the project is about to be tested by how fast the maintainer responds.

items.name: experientiallabs/world-model-optimizer
items.brief: On the HackerNews front page with points up 40.9% and comments up 22.7% in a day. Stars grew 18.6% but the watcher count sits at 1 against 255 stars — almost nobody has committed to following it. That gap is the thing to watch: front-page attention with no followers usually evaporates within the week.

items.name: mishushakov/desktui
items.brief: Appears in today's corroborated set on both GitHub and HackerNews. Early-stage terminal UI work, and like base-gpui the absolute numbers are small enough that the percentages overstate the case. Listed for completeness rather than conviction.

items.name: FrigadeHQ/yap
items.brief: Modest and clean — stars up 8% to 290, forks up 16%, 104 HackerNews points with 43 comments. Nothing here is dramatic, which is why it is worth noting: the numbers are in proportion to each other rather than one spiking alone.

items.name: SerhiiKorniienko/bullshit-detector
items.brief: Comments jumped 3,200% to 66 and points 178% to 62 — a one-to-one comment-to-point ratio, which almost always means argument rather than approval. Open issues rose 800% from a tiny base while stars grew 28%. It has already fallen off the front page, so the next two days decide whether the attention converts into anything.

items.name: wassgha/rescript
items.brief: Forks up 11% and open issues up 40% against 16% star growth, with 43 forks on 384 stars. That ratio is unusually high — better than one fork per nine stars — and suggests a tool people modify for their own use rather than adopt as-is.

items.name: openai/codex-security
items.brief: Forks up 70% and open issues up 84% against 47% star growth, reaching 6,090 stars and 399 forks. Issues climbing faster than stars is the signature of a repository people are running rather than reading, and at this size that means real deployments hitting real edges. On the HackerNews front page with 197 comments, which explains the arrival but not the fork ratio — that part is adoption.

items.name: gavamedia/deltafin
items.brief: Forks up 63% against 42% star growth, on the HackerNews front page with 87 comments. A fork-to-star ratio that high on a 429-star project means people are cloning to modify, not to bookmark. Open issues sitting at 1 says nobody has hit a wall yet, which is either a clean codebase or too early to tell.

items.name: twalichiewicz/HNewhere
items.brief: 419 HackerNews points with comments up 22%, but only 192 stars and 7 forks. Attention running far ahead of adoption: a lot of people found it interesting and very few took it home. It has left the front page, so this is close to its peak unless the star count starts closing the gap.

items.name: Freecash - Get Paid Real Money
items.brief: Freecash improved its best rank 4.9% to position 10 while losing ground in Germany, the UK and the US simultaneously. That combination means it charted hard somewhere outside the four markets tracked here. Paid-reward apps move on advertising budget, so read the climb as media spend rather than product adoption.
items.description: Pays people small amounts to complete offers, surveys and game milestones. Reward-app category, ad-funded.

items.name: Parchment: Agenda & Daily Note
items.brief: Parchment improved its best paid-chart rank 12% while falling in all three tracked paid markets, on just 124 ratings and a million Android installs. The rating count is far too small for the install figure, which usually means the Android and iOS audiences are very different sizes — worth checking before treating either number as the whole picture.

items.name: Claude by Anthropic
items.brief: Claude held the number one position across its tracked storefronts, gaining 3.6% in the UK while slipping slightly in Japan and the US. At 50 million Android installs and 215,000 ratings this is a competitive read rather than a discovery — the value is in which market moves which way, week to week.
